title: Latitudes and Longitudes: The Geographic Grid
tagline: Parallels and meridians, the important circles of latitude, local time and the International Date Line

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The latitude values, the time-zone rule of 15 degrees to the hour and the International Date Line behaviour are standard geodetic facts. No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Define latitude and longitude and state the value of the Equator and the Prime Meridian.
Locate the important parallels and meridians on the globe and state their latitudes and longitudes.
Calculate the time difference between two places using the 15 degrees to the hour rule.
Explain the purpose of the International Date Line and what happens when it is crossed.

overview.intro: Two sets of imaginary lines cover the globe and together form a grid. The lines running east to west are parallels of latitude, and they are circles of different sizes, the longest being the Equator and the shortest the Poles. The lines running north to south are meridians of longitude, and they are all equal semicircles that meet at the Poles. Latitude is the angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator, and longitude is the angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian at Greenwich. Because the Earth turns through 15 degrees of longitude every hour, the grid is also a clock: a place at 90 degrees east keeps its time six hours ahead of Greenwich, and a place at 90 degrees west keeps it six hours behind. The International Date Line, which follows the 180th meridian but is bent to keep whole countries on one side of it, is where the calendar date changes.

facts.label: Equator
facts.value: 0 degrees latitude, the longest parallel at about 40,075 km

facts.label: Prime Meridian
facts.value: 0 degrees longitude at Greenwich, the reference for all time zones

facts.label: Tropics and polar circles
facts.value: 23.5 degrees north and south; 66.5 degrees north and south

facts.label: Time rule
facts.value: The Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude every hour, so 1 degree equals 4 minutes

blocks.text: Parallels are imaginary circles drawn round the Earth from west to east. Each parallel is the set of all points at the same distance north or south of the Equator. The Equator is the longest parallel and divides the Earth into two equal halves, the Northern and the Southern Hemispheres. Towards the Poles the parallels become shorter and more closely spaced, because the meridians converge there. Latitude is the angular distance of any point on a parallel measured north or south of the Equator, and it is never greater than 90 degrees.

items.meaning: An imaginary circle round the Earth parallel to the Equator; all its points have the same latitude.
The angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator, measured from 0 to 90 degrees.
Latitude measured north of the Equator; the value is written with N after it.
Latitude measured south of the Equator; the value is written with S after it.

items: Parallels are circles of decreasing size from the Equator to the Poles.
The distance between two parallels that are 1 degree apart is about 111 km along a meridian.
The heat zones are marked out by the Tropics and the polar circles.
A place on the Tropic of Cancer has the Sun directly overhead at the June solstice.
Latitudes are written with N or S after the number, while longitudes are written with E or W.

blocks.text: Meridians are imaginary semicircles running from pole to pole, and every meridian is of the same length, about 20,004 km, that is half the circumference of the Earth. They are used to measure the longitude of a place, that is its angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, the meridian of 0 degrees longitude which passes through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in London. Every meridian meets every other meridian at both Poles, and the angle between two adjacent meridians is 1 degree of longitude.

items.meaning: An imaginary semicircle on the Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole, passing through the Equator.
The angular distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian, measured from 0 to 180 degrees.
The meridian of 0 degrees longitude, passing through Greenwich; the reference for all time zones.
An imaginary line near the 180th meridian, roughly following it but bent to keep the date and the day of the week uniform within a country.

items: Meridians are equal in length, unlike parallels.
All meridians converge at the North and South Poles.
The maximum value of longitude is 180 degrees, which is the meridian opposite the Prime Meridian.
The International Date Line is followed approximately by the 180th meridian but is deviated around some islands and countries.
Longitudes increase towards the east from the Prime Meridian and increase towards the west when written as West.

learn.title: Local time and the time zones

blocks.text: Because the Earth rotates from west to east, places further to the east see the Sun earlier, so their clocks are set ahead. The Earth turns through 15 degrees of longitude in one hour, because 360 degrees are covered in 24 hours. One degree of longitude therefore stands for 4 minutes of time. The mean time of the Prime Meridian is kept at Greenwich and is the standard for the whole world, and the local time of any place is worked out from its longitude and the time at Greenwich. In practice countries use time zones so that the clock on a railway timetable changes only at a boundary, and the zone boundaries are usually drawn along meridians.

blocks.caption: Table: converting longitude difference into time difference
rows: The greatest possible difference in local time

items.text: It is 10:00 a.m. at Greenwich. What is the local time at a place 75 degrees east?
items.note: 75 degrees is five zones east, so the time is 5 hours ahead: 10:00 a.m. plus 5 hours = 3:00 p.m. on the same day.

items.text: It is 4:00 p.m. at a place 90 degrees west of Greenwich. What is the time at Greenwich?
items.note: 90 degrees is six zones west, so Greenwich is 6 hours ahead of the place: 4:00 p.m. plus 6 hours = 10:00 p.m. on the same day.

items: Local time at a place = local time at Greenwich plus or minus the time difference, plus or minus the number of days if the date changes.
The countries that keep Greenwich Mean Time as their standard time include the United Kingdom, Ghana and Nigeria.
India keeps its standard time five and a half hours ahead of Greenwich, based on the meridian of 82.5 degrees east that passes through Mirzapur.
Time zones are numbered and named, for example UTC+2, and they exist so that neighbouring places share the same clock time.
The exact moment of sunrise is not the same as the start of the local day, which is conventionally 12:00 noon.

blocks.text: The International Date Line is an imaginary line on the surface of the Earth that separates two consecutive calendar dates. It follows the 180th meridian for most of its length but is bent wherever necessary so that a country and its islands are not split between two different days. Crossing the line from west to east, that is from Asia towards America, a traveller adds one day to the date, because the local time is gaining hours while the date has to be brought forward to keep the days in step. Crossing from east to west a traveller loses one day.

items.text: A ship sails east across the International Date Line on Tuesday 1 September. What is the date on the ship the moment it crosses to the eastern side?
items.note: Crossing westward to eastward gains a day, so the date becomes Wednesday 2 September. The clock time also advances by the local time difference, which is close to 12 hours at this line.

items.text: A traveller flies from Tokyo (140 degrees east) to Los Angeles (120 degrees west). Explain the change of date on arrival.
items.note: The flight crosses the International Date Line from west to east, so the traveller adds one day to the calendar date. The local time also falls by about 16 hours, because the difference in longitude is 260 degrees, that is 17 hours 20 minutes, taken as 16 hours forward and 1 hour 20 minutes back.

items: The date line is a convention of time keeping, not a physical boundary on the Earth.
It is bent near Alaska, near Russia and near New Zealand to avoid splitting those countries between two dates.
At the date line the local time difference is about 12 hours, the largest possible on the Earth.
Ships and aircraft must adjust the calendar date, and usually the clock as well, when they cross the line.
The line was first drawn by navigators so that the day of the week would not differ between the two halves of a voyage.

figures.caption: Figure: The geographic grid
figures.description: Parallels of latitude run east to west and are numbered from the Equator outwards; meridians of longitude run north to south and are numbered from the Prime Meridian outwards. The two sets cross at right angles and form a grid of squares and rectangles on the globe.

figures.description: The Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude in an hour, so each time zone covers 15 degrees of longitude and differs from Greenwich Mean Time by a whole number of hours, except where a country chooses a half-hour or three-quarter-hour offset.

keyPoints: Parallels are circles of latitude, meridians are semicircles of longitude, and the two together form the geographic grid.
The Equator is 0 degrees latitude and the Prime Meridian at Greenwich is 0 degrees longitude.
Latitude runs from 0 to 90 degrees north or south; longitude runs from 0 to 180 degrees east or west.
The Tropic of Cancer is 23.5 degrees N and the Tropic of Capricorn 23.5 degrees S.
The Arctic Circle is 66.5 degrees N and the Antarctic Circle 66.5 degrees S.
Parallels are unequal in length, meridians are equal, and all meridians meet at the Poles.
The Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude every hour, so 1 degree of longitude equals 4 minutes of time.
Local time at Greenwich is the standard for all time zones.
India keeps a standard time of UTC+5.5, based on the 82.5 degree east meridian.
Crossing the International Date Line from west to east gains a day; crossing it from east to west loses a day.
examFocus: Time questions always need three steps: work out the difference in longitude, convert it to minutes using 4 minutes per degree, then add or subtract it from the given time and state whether the date changes.
State the direction clearly: a place to the east of the given place has the later time, and a place to the west has the earlier time.
Recall questions on the grid usually ask for the latitude of the Equator, the Tropics, the polar circles and the longitude of the Prime Meridian and the date line; learn them as a set.
For a difference of more than 12 hours in longitude, remember that 180 degrees of longitude is the maximum possible difference of 12 hours.
When a question asks why the date line is bent, the answer is to keep the date and the day of the week the same throughout a country.

vocabulary.meaning: An imaginary circle of latitude running east to west around the Earth.
An imaginary semicircle of longitude running from pole to pole through the Equator.
The angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator, from 0 to 90 degrees.
The angular distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian, from 0 to 180 degrees.
The meridian of 0 degrees longitude passing through Greenwich.
The imaginary line near 180 degrees longitude where the calendar date changes.
The mean solar time of the Prime Meridian, used as the world standard time.
A band of longitude, usually 15 degrees wide, that keeps one standard time throughout.

questions.prompt: The latitude of the Tropic of Capricorn is:
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Capricorn lies 23.5 degrees south of the Equator. The Tropic of Cancer is the one at 23.5 degrees north.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 23.5 degrees N, which is the Tropic of Cancer.

questions.prompt: The Prime Meridian is the meridian of:
questions.explanation: The Prime Meridian at Greenwich is the reference line for longitude, so all longitudes are measured east or west from 0 degrees. The Equator is the reference for latitude.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 0 degrees latitude, which is the Equator rather than the Prime Meridian.

questions.prompt: One degree of longitude corresponds to a time difference of:
questions.explanation: The Earth turns 15 degrees of longitude in one hour, so 15 degrees equal 60 minutes and one degree equals 60 divided by 15, which is 4 minutes.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 15 minutes, which is the time for 15 degrees rather than for one degree.

questions.prompt: The International Date Line follows approximately the meridian of:
questions.explanation: The date line follows the 180th meridian, which is the meridian opposite the Prime Meridian, and is bent in a few places to keep countries whole.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 90 degrees, which is the meridian halfway between the Prime Meridian and the date line.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the latitude of the Arctic Circle is ________ degrees north.
questions.explanation: The Arctic Circle lies at 66.5 degrees north and the Antarctic Circle at 66.5 degrees south, and they bound the cold zones of the Earth.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 23.5 degrees, which is the latitude of the tropics.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the standard time of India is ______ hours ahead of Greenwich Mean Time.
questions.answer: 5 and a half hours ahead of Greenwich Mean Time, that is UTC+5.5
questions.explanation: India keeps its standard time on the meridian of 82.5 degrees east that passes through Mirzapur. That is 5.5 hours ahead of Greenwich, because 82.5 degrees at 4 minutes per degree gives 330 minutes, which is 5 hours 30 minutes.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 5 hours, which would correspond to the 75 degree east meridian and would leave half of India in the wrong time zone.

questions.prompt: State three differences between parallels of latitude and meridians of longitude.
questions.answer: Parallels are circles running east to west while meridians are semicircles running north to south. Parallels are unequal in length, being longest at the Equator and shortest at the Poles, whereas all meridians are equal in length. Parallels do not meet one another, while all meridians meet at the North and South Poles. Parallels are used to measure latitude north and south of the Equator, while meridians are used to measure longitude east and west of the Prime Meridian.
questions.explanation: A good comparison separates direction, shape, length and use.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only two differences, or repeating the same point in different words.

questions.prompt: Explain why the International Date Line is not a straight line along the 180th meridian.
questions.answer: The date line follows the 180th meridian for most of its length, but it is bent wherever a straight line would cut a country or a group of islands in two. The bends are made near Alaska, near Russia and near New Zealand so that the whole of each territory keeps the same calendar date and the same day of the week. Without these bends, one country would have two different days and two different days of the week at the same moment.
questions.explanation: The purpose of the line is a uniform calendar, so it is bent wherever the straight line would break a country apart.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the line is bent to follow a political boundary only, without giving the reason that the date must be uniform within a country.

questions.prompt: It is 6:00 a.m. on 10 January at a place 45 degrees west of Greenwich. Find the time and the date at Greenwich.
questions.answer: The difference in longitude is 45 degrees, and 45 x 4 = 180 minutes, so the time difference is 3 hours. The given place is west of Greenwich, so its clock is behind, and Greenwich is therefore 3 hours ahead: 6:00 a.m. plus 3 hours gives 9:00 a.m. on 10 January. The date does not change, because a difference of 3 hours is far too small to carry the time past midnight.
questions.explanation: Add the time difference in the right direction, and check afterwards whether the clock has passed midnight, which is what changes the date.
questions.commonMistake: Subtracting instead of adding, because the given place is to the west.

questions.prompt: It is 10:00 p.m. on 5 March at Greenwich. Find the local time and the date at a place 150 degrees east of Greenwich, and explain how the date is arrived at.
questions.answer: The difference in longitude is 150 degrees. At 4 minutes per degree this gives 150 x 4 = 600 minutes, which is 10 hours, so the place is 10 hours ahead of Greenwich. Adding 10 hours to 10:00 p.m. gives 8:00 a.m. The clock has passed midnight, so the date is one day later, that is 6 March. The date changes because the place is east of Greenwich and therefore sees the Sun earlier; the local date there has already moved on to the next day while it is still the previous evening at Greenwich.
questions.explanation: The three steps are the longitude difference, the conversion at 4 minutes per degree, and then the check for crossing midnight, which is what sets the date.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 8:00 a.m. without stating the date, or adding the ten hours and forgetting that midnight has been crossed.

questions.prompt: Explain why two places on the same parallel of latitude can have very different local times, and what would happen to their clock times if each used the time of the meridian through its own capital city instead.
questions.answer: Local time depends on longitude, not on latitude, because the Earth turns from west to east and so places further east see the Sun earlier. Two places on the same parallel, such as Paris and Moscow, or Delhi and Beijing, lie on the same line of latitude but can be many degrees of longitude apart, and each degree of longitude stands for 4 minutes of time. If each country instead kept the time of the meridian through its capital, each would set its clock to its own longitude, but the difference between the two clocks would then be the same as before in principle, because the time difference between two longitudes does not depend on which meridian each place chooses as its standard. The difference would only be reduced for the countries whose capitals are near the centre of their own territory, and the practical result would be an awkward clock time, for example half past midnight in the middle of the day, in countries that lie far from their capital meridian.
questions.explanation: Time is measured east to west by longitude, so a parallel has no single time, and the choice of standard meridian only decides where within a country the clock change falls.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming that places on the same parallel have the same time, which confuses latitude with longitude.
